extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and political history
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook treatment summarizing the framers' choices in drafting, ratifying, and later amending the U.S. Constitution, including the structural compromises, powers allocated to national and state governments, and the federal amending process. Intended as explanatory material for students learning constitutional design and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of minority rights against majority
rubrics_metrics.description: "the majority, having such coexistent passion or interest, must be rendered by their number and local situation unable to concert and carry into effect schemes of oppression"; the Constitution secured the rights of the minority against "the superior force of an interested and overbearing majority."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text presents Madisonian principle that constitutional structure should prevent majority factional oppression — achieved by institutional checks (separation of powers, staggered terms, different selection methods) rather than pure majority rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegates' latitude to exceed instructions in emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether delegates were bound by their instructions to amend the Articles or free to make a revolution in the political system; Randolph and Hamilton argued delegates could propose what they deemed necessary when "the salvation of the republic was at stake."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies the convention's decision to disregard strict instructions and draft a new instrument rather than only amend the Articles; treated as a legitimate constitutional practice in exigent circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of a supreme national (not merely federal) government
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution adopted that "a national government ought to be established consisting of a supreme legislative, executive, and judiciary." Gouverneur Morris: the national government has "a complete and compulsive operation" as opposed to a mere compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes centralizing authority to create enforceable, uniform national action rather than a loose league of sovereign states; motivates many other structural choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise on representation (Great Compromise / bicameralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small states demanded equal representation and large states representation by population; compromise: equality in the Senate and proportional representation in the lower House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bicameral design with different bases of representation was deliberate to balance competing state interests — used to reconcile area/population disparities among states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-fifths compromise on counting slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Slave states wished slaves counted in apportionment; compromise: "in apportioning representation and direct taxes only three-fifths of the total number of slaves should be counted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political bargain reflecting sectional interests; affected representation and taxation apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce and slave trade compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: North wanted Congress to regulate commerce; South feared prohibition of the slave trade if Congress had unqualified power; compromise authorized Congress to regulate commerce but forbade prohibition of importation of slaves before 1808.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits on congressional commerce power were negotiated to secure Southern ratification; demonstrates use of time-limited compromises to resolve sectional conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances through differentiated selection and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: President elected for four years by an indirect process; Senators elected for six years by state legislatures with staggered terms; Representatives elected by popular vote for two years; judges appointed for life by President and Senate with power to declare acts unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different modes of selection, term lengths, and life tenure for judges create institutional friction so no single party at one election can capture all branches and enact radical measures quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single energetic executive and method of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Convention concluded an executive department with a single head endowed with large powers; to allay fear of popular control, the President should be chosen indirectly by electors appointed as state legislatures might determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton's argument: "Energy in the executive is a leading character in the definition of good government" — combines strong authority with insulating election method to balance efficiency and protection against mob rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative reforms — bicameralism and national funding of members
rubrics_metrics.description: Three defects in Articles: equality of states in voting power, instability of a single chamber, and absence of direct representation. Convention provided a bicameral legislature and provided that members be paid from the national treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paying members from the national treasury was intended to remove dependence on state revenues and loyalties; direct popular election of the House was meant to provide representation of the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of a central judiciary and judicial review (as conceived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Old Congress lacked authority to organize courts of general jurisdiction; framers gave a Supreme Court and inferior courts jurisdiction over cases under the Constitution, laws, and treaties, and Hamilton feared courts should have power to declare laws unconstitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues courts were necessary to make laws effective, interpret treaties, and produce uniformity; this establishes the basis for later judicial review doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government deals directly with individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: New powers are given "special effectiveness" by authorizing the national government to deal with individuals instead of thirteen distinct states, preventing states from ignoring treaties or federal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts enforcement and legal effects from state-centric to individual-centric obligations, strengthening federal supremacy in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on state powers to protect national unity and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: States were forbidden to emit bills of credit; to make anything but gold and silver coin tender in payment; to pass ex post facto laws; to lay duties on imports or exports (except with Congress's consent for specific purposes); to lay tonnage duties; or to pass any law impairing the obligation of contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated prohibitions curtailed harmful interstate economic practices and preserved uniform national economic policy; designed to prevent states from undermining creditors, commerce, and treaty obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional financial and commercial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress authorized to raise revenues by taxes, duties, and excises bearing immediately upon the people; to regulate commerce among the several states and with foreign nations and Indians; authorized to establish uniform bankruptcy laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers remedied dependence on state legislatures for federal funds, ended interstate commercial warfare, and provided federal mechanisms (taxation, commerce regulation, bankruptcy) to stabilize national economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy of drafting (closed convention) as a procedural choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Convention sat behind closed doors; proceedings were secret and members were forbidden to correspond with outsiders on discussion topics so the draft would not be discovered and thwarted by public criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secrecy is presented as a deliberate tactic to allow candid bargaining and compromise in drafting a new instrument, albeit at cost of public transparency about framers' intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification by state conventions and nine-state rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Convention advised that the new Constitution be ratified by conventions in the several states chosen by the voters, and provided that when conventions of nine states had ratified the Constitution the new government should go into effect as far as those states were concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using popularly elected conventions rather than state legislatures aimed to root ratification in popular consent; the nine-state threshold made implementation possible without unanimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal amending process: methods and extraordinary thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Four possible ways of amending (practically one used): (1) proposition originates in Congress with two-thirds of both houses and ratified by legislatures or conventions in three-fourths of the states; (2) Congress must call a national convention on application of two-thirds of state legislatures to draft amendments, ratified likewise. The brief constitutional article leaves composition and procedure of such conventions unsettled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required extraordinary majorities for initiation and ratification make amendments difficult; Congress has historically been brief in amendment resolutions and left states discretion in approval procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: High amendment thresholds make ordinary amendment practically impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: "The system of amendment provided... requires such extraordinary majorities... that, in practice... no change has been made save under circumstances of a serious character." Burgess and other critics argue the requirement allows a minority to thwart the majority and may produce constitutional stress or revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual critique: the durability/stability of the Constitution is a double-edged sword — protections against capricious change also impede needed constitutional adaptation; historical changes often required extraordinary circumstances (e.g., war).
